name: The Jersey Devil
description: A winged, hoofed, horse-headed fiend said to haunt the Pine Barrens of New Jersey
origin: The Pine Barrens of southern New Jersey, USA

debut.title: The tale of Mother Leeds' thirteenth child
debut.era: 18th-century Pine Barrens lore; the great panic of January 1909

legend: The story goes that in 1735 a Pine Barrens woman called Mother Leeds, expecting her thirteenth child, cried that it might as well be the devil, and on a stormy night it was born with hooves, bat wings, a horse's head and a forked tail, and flew up the chimney. Historian Brian Regal traces the tale to a real family: Daniel Leeds, an almanac-maker whose astrology scandalised his Quaker neighbours, and whose son Titan put the family crest, with its dragon-like wyverns, on his almanac covers during a feud with Benjamin Franklin. The 'Leeds Devil' became the Jersey Devil during the panic of January 1909, when, over about a week, hundreds of people from Camden to Philadelphia reported strange tracks in the snow, screams in the night and glimpses of a flying thing. Schools and mills closed, posses went out, and the Philadelphia Zoo offered a reward. Publicist Norman Jeffries then exhibited a 'captured' Devil at Philadelphia's Arch Street Museum: a kangaroo with painted stripes and false wings, as he admitted twenty years later. Older stories claim Commodore Stephen Decatur fired a cannonball at it and that Joseph Bonaparte, Napoleon's brother, met it while hunting near Bordentown, though neither can be checked. Folklorists see a colonial feud that grew wings.

myths.claim: The legend says the Devil was Mother Leeds' thirteenth child.
myths.explanation: She is said to have cursed the unborn child, and it arrived in 1735 with hooves, wings and a horse's head before flying up the chimney.

myths.claim: The great Jersey Devil panic happened in 1909.
myths.explanation: For about a week in January 1909 sightings poured in from across the Delaware Valley, and some schools and mills closed.

myths.claim: A real Jersey Devil was captured and put on show in Philadelphia in 1909.
myths.explanation: Publicist Norman Jeffries exhibited a kangaroo with painted stripes and false wings at the Arch Street Museum, and admitted the hoax in 1929.

myths.claim: The creature was originally called the Leeds Devil.
myths.explanation: The older name points to the Leeds family of almanac-makers; 'Jersey Devil' took over around the time of the 1909 panic.

myths.claim: New Jersey's NHL team is named after it.
myths.explanation: When the franchise moved to New Jersey in 1982, fans voted to call it the Devils.

powers: A scream that empties a town
Leaving cloven tracks across rooftops and snow
Surviving cannon fire, so the story goes
legacy: The NHL's New Jersey Devils, named by a fan vote in 1982
The found-footage film The Last Broadcast (1998)
The Jersey Devil Coaster at Six Flags Great Adventure (2021)
facts: Legend says it was born to Mother Leeds in 1735 as her thirteenth child
It was first known as the Leeds Devil, after an almanac-making family of the Pine Barrens
Historian Brian Regal links the tale to the Leeds family crest, which shows dragon-like wyverns
In January 1909 hundreds of sightings across the Delaware Valley closed schools and mills
The Philadelphia Zoo offered a reward for its capture in 1909
A 'captured' Devil shown in Philadelphia in 1909 was a kangaroo with painted stripes and false wings
New Jersey's NHL team took its name from the creature after a fan vote in 1982
hostIntro: Tonight's guest was the thirteenth child, and you know how that goes. Hooves, wings, a horse's head: Mother Leeds really should have been more careful what she wished for.
